P2393.d: P2393 is the counterpart of P2392: one of the B-throttle motor leads has contact with battery voltage, for example through a pinched harness or a bridged pin in the connector, so the output stage sees an overcurrent as soon as it switches. No manufacturer publishes P2393.
s: MIL on
Filter regeneration not carried out
Possibly blown fuse or further circuit codes on the same supply
c: Motor lead pinched against a live wire or terminal
Bridged pins in the connector (moisture, corrosion)
Shorted turns in the throttle motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2394.d: P2394 means the B intake throttle remains wider open than requested even though the module drives its motor hard towards closing. A flap that cannot throttle fails to create the manifold depression that strong exhaust recirculation and regeneration heating depend on.
s: MIL on
Frequent or failing particulate filter regenerations
Engine shakes when switched off
c: Deposits holding the flap in an open position
Broken gear tooth or stripped drive between motor and shaft
Motor too weak to overcome the return spring
Foreign object or broken part blocking the flap

P2395.d: P2395 reports a B intake throttle that remains nearer to its closed stop than the module asks for. Of the two stuck faults this is the more serious one, because a flap jammed near its seat starves the engine of air.
s: Marked loss of power, limp mode
Black smoke under load
Rough running or stalling in severe cases
c: Deposits locking the flap near its closed stop
Broken return spring, flap no longer opens when unpowered
Jammed gear train or seized shaft bearing
Ice on the shaft or flap after cold, damp conditions

P2396.d: P2396 is the general electrical fault of the sensor that reports the angle of the B intake throttle, a potentiometer or, on newer units, a contactless Hall sensor with analogue or SENT output. The code says only that the signal is electrically implausible, without telling whether the reading sits under or over its window; makers that separate the two would set P2398 or P2399 instead.
s: MIL on
Flap switched off, EGR runs with limited control
Regeneration postponed
c: Damaged reference, ground or signal wire
Failed position sensor in the throttle unit

P2397.d: P2397 covers a B-throttle position signal that stays inside its electrical window but does not make sense, for instance a reading that does not move when the motor is driven, or one that disagrees with the commanded angle. CARB asks for such rationality checks on inputs wherever feasible.
s: MIL on
Displayed flap angle does not follow the command
Occasionally reduced power
c: Sticking flap that lags behind the command
Worn potentiometer track or drifting sensor
Contact resistance in connector or signal wire
Play between gear and flap shaft

P2398.d: P2398 is logged when the position signal of the B intake throttle falls below its lower limit. Likely reasons are a signal lead shorted to ground, a lost 5 V supply, or a broken signal wire that the module input pulls low; on SENT sensors the transmitted raw value can also leave its range.
s: MIL on
Further 5 V sensor codes at the same time
Regeneration suspended
c: Open 5 V reference or open signal wire
Shared 5 V reference pulled down by another faulty sensor

P2399.d: P2399 is the upper-limit counterpart of P2398: the B-throttle position signal reads higher than any real flap angle can produce. That usually points to a lost sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or water bridging the terminals in the connector.
s: MIL on
Flap stays at spring position
Regeneration suspended
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Moisture bridging terminals in the connector

P239A.d: P239A describes a B-throttle position signal that keeps jumping or dropping out for short moments, too briefly to set the low or high code. Loose terminals, a harness that cracks as the engine rocks, corrosion or a worn potentiometer track are typical; on digital SENT sensors corrupted messages have the same effect.
s: MIL that comes and goes
Short-lived jerks or EGR interruptions
Code stored without a permanent fault on testing
c: Loose or corroded terminals in the sensor connector
Wire breaking or rubbing intermittently with engine movement
Worn potentiometer track or faulty SENT sensor electronics
Electrical interference on the signal line

P239B.d: P239B checks the current the B-throttle motor draws while its H-bridge is switched on. A blocked or very stiff flap, a partly shorted winding or the two motor leads touching each other push the current beyond what the module expects.
s: MIL on
Flap switched off and resting at spring position
Often stored together with P2391 or the stuck codes
c: Flap blocked or very stiff, motor running at stall current
Short between the two motor leads in harness or connector
Faulty current measurement in the control module

P239C.d: P239C belongs to the air-mass control loop rather than to the throttle alone: with the B intake throttle taking part in that control, the module sees more fresh air than its target and cannot bring the reading down even at the limit of its authority. Too little recirculated exhaust gas is both the usual cause and the consequence, from an EGR valve stuck shut, a blocked EGR cooler, a flap that cannot close or an air-m
s: MIL on
No noticeable driving change in most cases
Often stored together with EGR flow codes
c: EGR valve stuck closed or EGR cooler clogged
B throttle unable to close far enough

P239D.d: P239D is the mirror image of P239C: the measured fresh-air mass remains below target although the control loop involving the B intake throttle is already at its limit. Candidates are an EGR valve that will not close and floods the intake with exhaust gas, a B flap stuck partly shut (often together with P2395), a restricted air filter or charge-air path, a turbocharger delivering too little, or an air-mass meter readi
s: Loss of power, possibly limp mode
Black smoke
Frequent particulate filter regenerations
c: Clogged air filter or restricted charge-air path
Contaminated air-mass meter reading too low

P239E.d: P239E carries in common code lists exactly the same wording as P232F: a downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 reading outside its expected window while fuel is cut on deceleration. No manufacturer, OBD summary or service bulletin on record uses P239E, and no source gives it a meaning of its own.
s: MIL on without noticeable driving change
Code text in the scan tool contradicts the manufacturer's documentation
c: Scan tool code table showing the duplicate number instead of the maker's code
Aged or drifting rear oxygen sensor on bank 1
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor

P239F.d: P239F appears in code lists with the identical title already given to P2379: the post-catalyst oxygen sensor of bank 2 is out of range while the injectors are switched off on a closed throttle. Neither code has a published manufacturer application; the only documented member of this deceleration check is GM's bank 1 code P232F on the single-bank 2023 L5P diesel, so a second bank never occurs there.
s: MIL on, engine runs normally
Catalyst monitor may not complete
c: Scan tool listing the duplicate number for a maker-specific fault
Aged rear oxygen sensor on bank 2
Air leak in the bank 2 exhaust ahead of the sensor

P23A0.d: P23A0 repeats, word for word, the title of P237A in the usual code lists: the rear oxygen sensor of bank 1 does not see, or does not report, a representative sample of post-catalyst exhaust. No manufacturer uses P23A0 in any published OBD table or service bulletin, and no source defines it differently, so it is a duplicate listing of P237A.
s: MIL on, no drivability change
Catalyst diagnosis unreliable or incomplete
c: Scan tool code table using the duplicate number
Air leak in the exhaust ahead of the rear sensor on bank 1
Sensor mounted poorly or element contaminated

P23A1.d: P23A1 is listed with the same title as P237B: the bank 2 oxygen sensor behind the catalyst reports something that cannot be genuine exhaust from that bank. Only engines with two exhaust banks and a downstream sensor on each side could produce it.
s: MIL on, engine runs normally
Readiness for catalyst monitor stays open
c: Scan tool reporting the duplicate number
Leak in the bank 2 exhaust pipe ahead of the rear sensor
Damaged wiring or connector of the bank 2 rear sensor

P23A2.d: P23A2 reports an open or otherwise broken drive circuit for the second exhaust bypass flap, valve B, of an exhaust heat exchanger. Such units route the exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and send it past once engine and cabin are warm; a valve B only exists where the layout needs two flaps.
s: Check engine light on
Slower engine and cabin warm-up in cold weather
No change in how the vehicle drives
c: Connector at the valve B actuator loose, corroded or unplugged
Control wire broken near the hot exhaust or at a harness clip
Actuator coil or internal electronics of valve B open

P23A3.d: With P23A3 the module sees the control line of exhaust bypass valve B sitting lower than its commanded state allows, which usually means that the wire or the driver stage of the actuator has found a path to ground. Water or road salt in a connector under the vehicle is a typical trigger.
s: Check engine light on
Heater output builds up slowly after a cold start
Fault may reappear after rain or washing
c: Control wire chafed through and touching body or exhaust ground
Moisture or salt bridging pins in the actuator connector
Internal short in the valve B actuator

P23A4.d: P23A4 is stored when the control circuit of exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve B reads higher than expected – a short to a battery feed, a chafed wire touching another supply, or an actuator whose electronics pull the line up. Because the flap no longer obeys, the warm-up strategy has to run without it.
s: Check engine light on
Bypass flap does not respond to an actuator test
Driving behaviour unchanged
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Failed electronics inside the valve B actuator
Output stage in the controlling module faulty

P23A5.d: Unlike the circuit codes, P23A5 judges the result: the module commanded valve B, the second exhaust bypass at the heat exchanger, but it does not see the response it expects, for example in position feedback or in how the exhaust-side coolant temperatures change. No manufacturer publishes P23A5.
s: Check engine light on
Cabin heat slow to arrive in winter
No effect on drivability
c: Flap of valve B sluggish from soot or corrosion
Exhaust coolant temperature sensor connector wet or corroded, distorting the plausibility check
Overly strict calibration, fixed by a software update

P23A6.d: P23A6 says that bypass valve B of the exhaust heat exchanger stays open while the module wants it closed. In the usual layout the exhaust then keeps taking the bypass route, so the heat exchanger adds little or no heat after a cold start – noticeable as a slow engine warm-up and a weak cabin heater in cold weather, and on hybrids as the engine running longer just to make heat.
s: Check engine light on
Engine and heater take noticeably longer to warm up
Hybrid engine runs more often in cold weather
c: Flap seized in the open position by carbon or corrosion
Linkage between actuator and flap broken or detached
Actuator no longer able to move the flap

P23A7.d: P23A7 is the opposite of P23A6: the second bypass valve (B) on the exhaust heat exchanger does not open on command and stays closed. Depending on the layout, all exhaust is then forced through the heat exchanger even when the engine is fully warm, which adds heat to the coolant and some back pressure – most relevant under load and in hot weather.
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature higher than usual under load
Possibly reduced power or a changed exhaust note
c: Flap stuck closed by deposits or corrosion
Damaged or water-filled heat exchanger obstructing the flap

P23A8.d: P23A8 concerns the position feedback of exhaust bypass valve B at its mechanical end stops. Systems with a position sensor learn the readings at the fully open and the fully closed stop and compare later readings with them; if a stop value drifts out of its window, or the flap no longer reaches the stop at all, this code is set.
s: Check engine light on
Valve position in live data does not reach the expected end value
c: Deposits or a bent flap keep valve B from reaching its end stop
Position sensor in the actuator drifted or loose
End stops not relearned after a repair

P23A9.d: P23A9 records that the engine was stopped, or kept from running, because the engine module lost contact with a control unit whose messages it needs to operate the engine safely. The title names only the consequence; which data link is meant is defined by each manufacturer, and none publishes P23A9.
s: Engine stops while driving or does not start
Several U codes and warning messages from other modules
MIL or other warning lights on
c: Damaged CAN wiring, connector or termination
Partner module without power or ground, or low battery voltage
Failed or wrongly programmed partner module
Software versions of the modules not matching after repair

P23AA.d: P23AA concerns bypass valve A of a turbocharger or supercharger, which opens a path around the compressor to relieve boost when the throttle closes or at part load. The code means the valve no longer follows its command and sits fixed.
s: Reduced boost and power
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off
MIL on, possibly limited power mode
c: Valve or actuator mechanically seized (deposits, wear)
Faulty electric actuator or position sensor of the valve
High resistance in wiring or connector

P23AB.d: A NOx sensor is a smart part: the probe in the exhaust is wired to a small control unit with its own processor, which runs the heater, evaluates the cell currents and reports over CAN. P23AB means that this electronics in sensor 3 of bank 1 – usually the one behind a second SCR catalyst – reports an internal error or fails its self-checks.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 values missing or frozen in live data
SCR or emissions warning on the display
c: Internal electronics of the sensor 3 control unit defective
Supply voltage dips or poor ground resetting the sensor electronics
Sensor control unit damaged by heat or water ingress

P23AC.d: P23AC is the general electrical fault reported for NOx sensor 3 on bank 1. The sensor's own control unit watches the leads between its electronics and the ceramic probe and tells the engine computer over CAN whether a measuring circuit is open or shorted; the user manual of Drivven's NOx sensor module kit, published by NI, lists these status states for the NOx and O2 circuits.
s: Check engine light on
No NOx reading from sensor 3 in live data
SCR system warning
c: Lead between probe and sensor control unit damaged by heat or chafing
Corroded or loose terminals at the sensor 3 connectors
Probe or sensor electronics failed internally

P23AD.d: P23AD flags the third NOx sensor on bank 1 as electrically intact but not trustworthy. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes the check for its post-second-catalyst NOx sensor: the internal stability flags of the NOx and lambda current control are watched, and a flag counts as off when, for instance, the V2 cell voltage leaves a 40 mV band around its set point or the pump currents Ip1 and Ip2 change faster than a
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 NOx value jumps in live data
SCR efficiency monitor may not complete
c: Aged or poisoned sensing cell giving unstable pump currents
High contact resistance in the sensor 3 wiring
Exhaust leak near the sensor upsetting the measurement

P23AE.d: P23AE is set when the third NOx sensor on bank 1 reports a concentration below anything physically possible. GM's 25OBDG04B table for its 2025 diesels requires the raw NOx value of the sensor behind the second catalyst to fall under −90 ppm in 100 of 200 samples, taken every 25 ms once dew point is reached, supply exceeds 9.9 V and no CAN fault is present; it is rated Type B with the MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Negative or zero NOx value for sensor 3 in live data
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time
c: Engine harness chafed, disturbing the sensor 3 supply or signal
Sensor 3 with a negative offset from ageing or damage

P23AF.d: With P23AF the third NOx sensor on bank 1 delivers a value above its measuring range. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B sets the code when the raw reading of the post-second-catalyst sensor exceeds 2,990 ppm in 120 of 240 samples, provided the air system control is active or DEF dosing is ready; the rating is Type B, so the MIL follows on the second trip.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 shows implausibly high NOx even at idle
SCR efficiency code may follow
c: Wire broken inside the insulation near a connector in the exhaust sensor harness
Sensor 3 failed with a reading stuck high
Short between sensor lines in the harness

P23B0.d: P23B0 is meant for a third NOx sensor on bank 1 whose circuit faults come and go instead of staying present, so the status the sensor module reports over CAN keeps toggling between valid and faulty. No manufacturer documents P23B0 publicly, and none publishes a threshold for it; GM's 2025 diesel table, which details several other sensor 3 codes, does not list it.
s: Check engine light that goes out and returns
Sensor 3 value drops out briefly in live data
c: Loose or fretting terminal in a sensor 3 connector
Harness rubbing or flexing near the exhaust, breaking contact under vibration
Moisture entering a connector in wet weather

P23B1.d: A NOx sensor only measures once its built-in heater has brought the ceramic element up to temperature. P23B1 reports that the heater control side of the third sensor on bank 1 is open.
s: Check engine light after one trip
Sensor 3 never reports operating temperature
SCR warning on the display
c: Heater element in the sensor 3 probe burnt through
Broken heater conductor between probe and sensor module
Probe connector not fully engaged after a repair

P23B2.d: P23B2 points to the heater control line of bank 1's NOx sensor 3 being pulled to ground. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B checks that pin on the sensor downstream of the second catalyst for a short to ground and, unlike the open-circuit test, waits until the dew point has been reached, so that the heater is actually allowed to run; 80 failed out of 160 samples set the code.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 slow or unable to become ready
c: Heater control wire chafed against ground
Internal short in the heater of sensor 3
Water bridging the heater pins in the connector

P23B3.d: If, on NOx sensor 3 of bank 1, the heater control pin sits at supply voltage when the electronics expect it to switch, P23B3 is stored. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes it, for the sensor behind the second catalyst, as a battery short at the heater drive pin, evaluated every 25 ms with sensor supply above 9.9 V and dew point reached, and failing at 80 of 160 samples; Type B with the MIL on the second trip.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 heater status shows an error in live data
SCR warning
c: Heater control wire shorted to a supply line
Heater driver inside the sensor 3 electronics failed

P23B4.d: Besides its drive line, the heater of a NOx sensor has a sense connection through which its resistance, and with it the element temperature, is measured. P23B4 reports a fault in that sense path for the third sensor on bank 1.
s: Check engine light after one trip
Sensor 3 temperature status invalid
c: Heater sense lead broken between probe and module
Backed-out or corroded terminal at the probe connector
Internal break in the sensor 3 probe

P23B5.d: P23B5 says the heater feedback from NOx sensor 3 (bank 1) is present but implausible: the element does not reach or hold the resistance that matches its target temperature. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B compares the raw heater resistance of the post-second-catalyst sensor with its target and fails it outside a relative band of 0.06, after waiting 200 s from supply in range and from dew point; 125 of 250 samples, T
s: Check engine light after one trip
Several NOx sensor and communication codes at once
SCR warning, sensor 3 not ready
c: NOx sensor harness chafing on a hot component such as the EGR cooler (Ford 2023 6.7L)
Aged heater element whose resistance no longer matches the target
Blown fuse in the NOx sensor supply after a short
High contact resistance in the heater connector

P23B6.d: P23B6 concerns the power feed of the third NOx sensor on bank 1, the smart probe behind the second SCR catalyst. Its built-in control unit needs a stable supply, and when the voltage it reports leaves the allowed range the engine module stores this code.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 shows no NOx value in live data
Further NOx sensor or communication codes stored at the same time
c: Blown fuse in the NOx sensor supply after a short elsewhere in the harness
Supply or ground wire chafed through on the engine or frame (GM 3.0L LM2)
Corroded or loose pins in the sensor 3 connector under the vehicle
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the sensor supply down

P23B7.d: P23B7 is set when the heater drive of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 looks electrically sound but does not behave as the control strategy expects, for instance a heater duty cycle far from what the element should need to reach operating temperature. No manufacturer documents P23B7 publicly; GM's 2025 table covers sensor 3 only with the plain heater circuit codes P23B1-P23B3 and the resistance check P23B5.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 takes long to become ready or drops out of its active state
SCR efficiency monitor not completing
c: Aged heater element that needs far more or less power than expected
High resistance in heater supply or ground contacts
Sensor supply voltage at the lower limit, so the heater cannot keep up

P23B8.d: Smart NOx sensors report heater temperature through a separate sense connection, which GM calls the HTemp pin. P23B8 means this line on sensor 3 of bank 1 is pulled to ground.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 does not report valid NOx values
Often stored together with other wiring-related codes
c: Sense wire chafed through and touching body, frame or exhaust ground
Water or salt bridging the sense pin to ground in the connector
Internal short in the sensor or its control unit

P23B9.d: P23B9 is the counterpart of P23B8: the temperature feedback wire of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 carries a voltage that only a short to battery or to another live wire can explain. The sensor then cannot report a trustworthy heater temperature, so it withholds its NOx output.
s: Check engine light after two trips
No NOx reading from sensor 3
Possibly a blown fuse in the sensor supply
c: Sense wire shorted to the heater supply or another battery-fed wire
Harness insulation melted by contact with hot exhaust parts
Internal fault in the sensor or its control unit

P23BA.d: With P23BA, the heater feedback signal from the third NOx sensor of bank 1 keeps vanishing or leaping for a moment and then recovers, rather than staying broken. P23BA itself is not described in any public manufacturer document.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Sensor 3 briefly leaves its ready state
Fault often cannot be reproduced in the workshop
c: Terminal in the sensor 3 connector with weak contact pressure
Sense lead cracked by vibration or heat and opening only at times
Moisture entering the plug through a damaged seal

P23BB.d: P23BB says the heater element of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 has a resistance outside its permitted band. Because the resistance of the ceramic heater climbs with temperature, it doubles as the thermometer of the probe, so an aged or cracked element heats poorly and reports a false temperature as well.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 slow to become ready after a cold start
Implausible NOx readings from the rear sensor
c: Heater element aged by long service at high exhaust temperature
Element cracked by water droplets hitting the hot ceramic
Added resistance from a corroded heater contact

P23BC.d: Every smart NOx sensor carries its own control unit with a memory holding trim and reference data written for that individual probe at the factory. P23BC means this memory in sensor 3 on bank 1 cannot be read or fails its integrity check, so the engine module can no longer trust the readings.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 readings ignored by the engine module
SCR monitoring cannot complete
c: Memory inside the sensor control unit corrupted or failed
Voltage dips or spikes on the sensor supply disturbing the memory
Replacement sensor with a calibration that does not match the vehicle

P23BD.d: P23BD means NOx sensor 3 on bank 1, the last probe downstream of the second SCR catalyst, reports more NOx than the operating state allows, or its value no longer comes down from a high level. A common test is engine overrun without fuel, when the exhaust contains no NOx at all: Volvo, for its inlet-sensor counterpart P225C, expects the reading to fall below 50 ppm within roughly 10 s.
s: Check engine light on
SCR efficiency code may follow although the catalyst is fine
Sensor 3 reading stays high in overrun
c: Measuring cell drifted upward with age or contamination
Monitor calibration too strict, fixed by an engine software update
Sensor element damaged by thermal shock or poisoning

P23BE.d: P23BE is the low-side mirror of P23BD: NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 shows less NOx than is plausible, or it stays near zero while the engine is clearly producing some. Behind a working SCR system the true value is small anyway, which makes a low-stuck sensor the more dangerous error for monitoring, because it can hide a failing catalyst.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 reads near zero under load
Possibly an audible exhaust leak at the rear section
c: Exhaust leak or air drawn in ahead of sensor 3, diluting the gas
Measuring cell lost sensitivity and reads too low
Sensor not seated correctly so it samples too little exhaust

P23BF.d: P23BF concerns how quickly NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 follows a rise in NOx. The control module waits for an increasing transient and times the climb of the sensor signal against what a model predicts.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 signal trails the front sensor during acceleration
No change in how the engine runs
c: Soot, oil ash or urea residue blocking the gas inlet of the sensor
Measuring cells aged beyond their response specification
Element running too cold because the heater is weak

P23C0.d: With P23C0 the third NOx sensor on bank 1 is too sluggish when NOx falls, for instance when the driver lifts off and the engine goes into fuel cut-off. The module measures how long the reading takes to come down between two levels.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 value stays raised for seconds after lifting off
Driveability unaffected
c: Deposits from condensate, fuel or oil on the sensor element
Holes in the protective tube partly blocked by soot or urea crystals
Sensor aged and no longer able to release its reading quickly

P23C1.d: P23C1 asks whether the measuring cells of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 have lost sensitivity, for example because deposits clog the internal cavities. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B runs the test on the post-second-catalyst sensor during afterrun: the sensor shifts its internal pump currents so that oxygen in the second cavity rises to a target, and the outcome is set against a value the supplier recorded on the new part and wr
s: Check engine light after one trip
SCR monitoring results become unreliable
No noticeable change in engine behaviour
c: Internal measuring cavities clogged by ash or other deposits
Sensing cells worn out after high mileage
Wiring fault upsetting the sensor supply during the test (GM 3.0L LM2)

P23C2.d: P23C2 targets the dead time of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 when NOx drops: the reading only starts to fall too long after the exhaust has changed, even if it then moves at a normal pace. CARB separates these two failure types in its oxygen sensor definitions, calling the time before a sensor first reacts delayed response and a sluggish transition slow response.
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 value holds briefly before dropping in overrun
Engine runs normally
c: Protective tube partly blocked, so new exhaust gas reaches the cell late
Aged sensing cells reacting late to a change
Condensate in the sensor housing after many short trips

P23C3.d: P23C3 is the general electrical fault on the feedback sensor that tells the engine module how far the third coolant bypass valve has turned. On modern thermal management modules this valve is a motor-driven rotary part, so without a valid angle the module loses its closed-loop positioning.
s: Engine warning lamp
Engine takes longer to reach operating temperature
Coolant temperature gauge reads unusually high or unsteady
c: Loose, corroded or coolant-contaminated connector at the valve module
Damaged signal, 5 V reference or ground wire of the position sensor
Internal failure of the position sensor built into the valve actuator
Faulty sensor input or reference supply in the engine control module

P23C4.d: P23C4 says the angle reported by the bypass valve C position sensor has dropped below anything the sensor can produce in normal use, which GM traces to the signal line touching ground. GM's 2025 tables use the code on both its 3.0L Duramax diesel (25OBDG04B) and a gasoline family (25OBDG03B): the SENT sensor value must fall under 27 or under 50 counts respectively, for 4 seconds within a 5-second window, while SENT c
s: Engine warning lamp after two drives
Bypass valve C position shown as implausibly low in live data
Slow warm-up or unusual engine temperature
c: Position sensor signal wire chafed against ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector bridging the signal to ground
Defective position sensor inside the valve actuator
Missing sensor supply so the output stays at its lowest value

P23C5.d: With P23C5 the position feedback of coolant bypass valve C sits at the top end of its digital range, a reading GM explains as the signal line touching a voltage source. In GM's 2025 summaries for the 3.0L Duramax (25OBDG04B) and a gasoline engine family (25OBDG03B) the limit is identical: a SENT value above 4,050 counts present for 4 seconds within 5 seconds, checked only when the SENT link reports no error and the e
s: Engine warning lamp on the second faulty trip
Live data shows bypass valve C near full scale regardless of command
Heater output or engine temperature behaves unusually
c: Position signal wire shorted to a supply or reference wire
Open ground wire of the position sensor
Position sensor in the valve actuator reporting a stuck maximum value
Bent or spread terminals in the valve connector

P23C6.d: P23C6 is set by the output stage itself: the H-bridge that drives the motor of coolant bypass valve C reports more current, or more heat, than it can tolerate. GM labels it a motor overcurrent in two 2025 summaries, the diesel table 25OBDG04B (3.0L Duramax) and the gasoline table 25OBDG03B; the driver flags it while energized, with a controller-specific trip point listed between 8.1 and 12.8 A, and the code matures a
s: Engine warning lamp after two trips
Bypass valve C no longer moves and stays in its last position
Engine runs too cold or too warm depending on where the valve stopped
c: Valve rotor stiff or seized by deposits or worn seals, so the motor stalls
Shorted windings in the valve motor drawing excess current
Motor wires partly shorted to each other or to ground
Overheated or faulty H-bridge driver in the engine control module

P23C7.d: Flex-fuel engines that must start on high-ethanol blends in the cold warm the fuel before injection, and a separate heating control unit switches the high heater currents on command of the engine module. P23C7 reports that the power control line to this unit is open or electrically faulty, so the heaters cannot be enabled.
s: Hard or failed cold starts on high ethanol blends
Rough running right after a cold start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Broken or disconnected power control wire between engine module and heater unit
Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the heater control circuit
Corroded or loose connector at the fuel heater control module
Internal fault in the fuel heater control module

P23C8.d: P23C8 covers the case where the engine module finds the heater unit's power control line pulled to ground. The likely culprit is a chafed wire touching the body or engine, or a short inside the heater unit.
s: Long cranking in cold weather on ethanol
Blown fuse in the fuel heater circuit
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Power control wire chafed through to ground
Moisture in the heater unit connector creating a path to ground
Shorted control input inside the fuel heater control module
Faulty output driver in the engine control module

P23C9.d: P23C9 is stored when the power control line to the fuel heater control unit shows battery voltage although the engine module has it switched off, pointing to a short to a live wire. The real risk here is the reverse of the low case: the heater stage may be enabled without being asked, warming the fuel after it is no longer needed and loading the electrical system.
s: Fuel heating active when not needed, possible battery drain
Heater unit or wiring gets unusually warm
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Power control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Welded relay contact keeping the circuit energized
Internal leakage in the fuel heater control module
Engine module output that does not switch off

P23CA.d: Some flex-fuel engines heat the fuel directly in the injector rail: a heating element in the rail brings ethanol up to temperature just before a cold start. P23CA flags the control circuit of that rail heater as open or otherwise faulty, so no heating current flows.
s: No start or long cranking on ethanol below about 13 °C
Misfiring or stumbling in the first seconds after a cold start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Burnt-out heating element in the fuel rail
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the rail heater
Corroded high-current terminals at the heater
Failed output stage in the fuel heater control module

P23CB.d: P23CB means the control side of the fuel rail heater reads too low, normally a short to ground between the switching stage and the heating element. Since a rail heater draws a high current, a ground short on its feed can blow the fuse or trip the protection in the driving stage before the fuel gets warm.
s: Difficult cold start with ethanol
Fuel heater fuse blows repeatedly
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Heater feed wire chafed to ground near the intake manifold
Heating element shorted to the rail body
Fuel or water in the heater connector
Shorted output stage in the fuel heater control module

P23CC.d: With P23CC the fuel rail heater control circuit sits at supply voltage when it should not, most often because the line has shorted to a battery feed or the switching element is stuck conducting. The concern is uncontrolled heating: if the element keeps running, the fuel in the rail can get hotter than intended once the engine is warm.
s: Rail heater stays on after start
Hard restart when the engine is hot
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Heater control wire shorted to a battery feed
Switching transistor in the heater unit stuck conducting
Internal fault in the fuel heater control module
Damaged terminals letting adjacent pins touch

P23CD.d: Besides being commanded, a fuel heater control unit reports back to the engine module, so the engine knows whether heating actually took place. P23CD indicates that this feedback line carries no usable signal or is open.
s: Cold-start fuel heating disabled or unconfirmed
Harder starts on ethanol in cold weather
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Broken feedback wire between heater unit and engine module
Loose or corroded pin for the feedback signal
Heater unit without supply or ground, so it sends nothing
Failed feedback output in the fuel heater control module

P23CE.d: Unlike the open and short codes, P23CE concerns a feedback signal that is electrically present but does not fit what the engine module expects. The heater unit may, for example, report no temperature rise during a commanded heating phase, a rise that is far too slow, or values that contradict the command state.
s: Slow or rough cold starts on ethanol without a wiring fault
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Aged heating element delivering less heat than commanded
High resistance at heater power or ground terminals
Drifting temperature or current measurement inside the heater unit
Weak battery reducing heating power during cranking

P23CF.d: P23CF is logged when the feedback line from the fuel heater control unit stays near ground, below its valid signal range. Mostly the wire is chafed against ground or the feedback output inside the unit is shorted.
s: Fuel heating not used for cold starts
Long cranking with ethanol in cold weather
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Moisture in a connector of the feedback circuit
Shorted feedback output in the fuel heater control module
Faulty input stage in the engine control module

P23D0.d: P23D0 applies when the return signal from the fuel heater control unit is stuck above its plausible maximum. A short to a voltage source on the feedback wire is the usual explanation; with a pull-up input in the engine module an open ground at the heater unit can produce the same picture.
s: Fuel heating switched off as a precaution
Poor cold starts on high ethanol blends
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Feedback wire shorted to a voltage supply
Missing ground at the fuel heater control module
Feedback output of the heater unit stuck high
Faulty input stage in the engine control module

P23D1.d: Instead of one heater for the whole rail, some flex-fuel systems give every cylinder its own heating path, either a heated injector or an element at each rail outlet. P23D1 is the open or general circuit fault on the path for cylinder 1, so that cylinder gets unheated ethanol during a cold start.
s: Cylinder 1 misfire right after a cold start on ethanol
Rough idle until the engine warms up
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Burnt-out heater at cylinder 1 (heated injector or rail element)
Broken wire or unplugged heater connector at cylinder 1
Corroded terminals in the cylinder 1 heater connector
Failed channel 1 output in the fuel heater control module

P23D2.d: P23D2 is the high-voltage fault on the cylinder 1 heater circuit; note that in this series the high code comes before the low code (P23D3). The control side of the heater shows supply voltage while it should be switched off, so the switching stage has lost control: a short to a positive wire or a switching element that no longer turns off are the usual reasons.
s: Cylinder 1 heater stays on, higher current draw
Possible hot-restart problems
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 1 heater control wire shorted to a positive feed
Channel 1 switching element stuck on in the heater unit
Damaged connector letting the heater pin touch a supply pin

P23D3.d: P23D3 reports that the control circuit of the cylinder 1 fuel heater is pulled toward ground. It follows the high code P23D2 in the numbering, not the other way round.
s: Single-cylinder misfire on cold ethanol starts
Blown fuse in the fuel heater circuit
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 1 heater wire chafed to ground on the intake or engine
Heater at cylinder 1 shorted to its housing
Fuel or water in the cylinder 1 heater connector
Shorted channel 1 output in the heater unit

P23D4.d: P23D4 is not about wiring at all: the cylinder 1 heater circuit is electrically intact, yet it fails to heat as it should. The heater unit measures what each heat circuit delivers, so a heater that draws too little current, warms too slowly or reaches a lower temperature than its neighbours stands out.
s: Cylinder 1 runs rough for a while after a cold start on ethanol
Longer cranking in cold weather
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Aged cylinder 1 heater with reduced heating power
High-resistance connection in the cylinder 1 heater circuit
Deposits reducing heat transfer at a heated injector
Low battery voltage during the heating phase

P23D5.d: Cylinder 2 has its own fuel heating path on flex-fuel engines that warm the fuel per cylinder, and P23D5 says this path carries no current although the heater is commanded on, or the control line shows a general fault. To the heater unit the open simply looks like a missing load on channel 2.
s: Cylinder 2 misfires briefly after a cold start on ethanol
Uneven idle in the first minute when cold
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Heater at cylinder 2 burnt through (open element)
Cylinder 2 heater plug loose or not latched after intake work
Broken conductor in the cylinder 2 heater lead
Channel 2 output of the heater control unit failed

P23D6.d: P23D6 flags the control circuit of the cylinder 2 fuel heater as high. A heater driver typically checks the line both with the channel off and with it on; a level that stays near supply voltage in both states points to a control wire touching a positive feed or to a driver that no longer pulls the circuit down.
s: Heater at cylinder 2 runs on or does not switch
Cylinder 2 starts cold on ethanol
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 2 heater control wire touching a positive feed
Switching FET of channel 2 failed in the conducting state
Bent connector pin touching a supply terminal

P23D7.d: For P23D7 the module reads the cylinder 2 heater control line as low, which on these power circuits nearly always means a path to ground: a chafed wire, a heater element shorted to its body, or fuel or water bridging the connector pins. The short draws more than the channel is meant to carry, so the heater unit protects itself; Bosch mentions reverse-voltage and internal overtemperature protection as well as short de
s: Rough cold start on one cylinder
Fuel heater fuse blown
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 2 heater wire chafed through to ground
Heating element at cylinder 2 shorted to its housing
Fuel or water bridging pins in the cylinder 2 heater plug

P23D8.d: P23D8 concerns how well the cylinder 2 heater works, not its wiring. According to Bosch, the Flexstart heated rail warms pure ethanol fuel at rates of as much as 30 °C a second, so a system of this kind knows roughly how quickly each heating point ought to warm up.
s: Cylinder 2 runs rough for about a minute after a cold ethanol start
Longer cranking below freezing
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 2 heater element with reduced output
Varnish or scale on the heated surface at cylinder 2
Corroded contact dropping voltage under heater load

P23D9.d: P23D9 is the open-circuit or general circuit fault of the heating path for cylinder 3. The fuel heater control unit drives each heater through a channel of its own; when channel 3 is switched on but no load current appears, the connection to the heater is considered broken.
s: Stumble on cylinder 3 after a cold ethanol start
Harder starting below about 13 °C
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Terminal pushed out of the cylinder 3 heater connector
Wire broken where the harness flexes near the rail
Failed channel 3 output in the heater unit

P23DA.d: P23DA tells that the control side of the cylinder 3 heater sits at a high level. The likely pictures are a control wire touching a positive feed, so voltage stays on the line when the channel is off, or an output stage that has failed conducting, so heater 3 runs without command.
s: Flat battery after the car has stood for some hours
Heater at cylinder 3 warm long after switch-off
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 3 control wire shorted to a positive feed

P23DB.d: With P23DB the cylinder 3 heater control circuit is too low, meaning the line or the heater itself has found a path to ground. Because a single heat circuit is sized for several hundred watts, such a short trips the current limit at once; Bosch describes short detection per circuit and an integrated current relay in its Flexstart unit, which then cuts only the affected channel.
s: One-cylinder roughness when starting cold
Other cylinders start normally
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Water in the cylinder 3 heater connector
Harness chafed through at a damaged clip near the rail
Heated injector at cylinder 3 shorted internally

P23DC.d: P23DC is set when the heating at cylinder 3 works electrically but delivers too little effect. Bosch writes that its heater unit follows the heat output of all four circuits and hands a temperature reading to the engine controller, so a channel that warms more weakly than the others can be singled out.
s: Misfire on cylinder 3 during warm-up on ethanol
Lean running in the first minutes
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Cylinder 3 heating element below its rated output
High-resistance crimp or plug in the cylinder 3 heater circuit

P23DD.d: P23DD reports an open or general fault on the fourth and last heating channel. Bosch builds its heater unit with exactly four heat circuits and its heated rail for either three- or four-cylinder operation, so this code belongs to four-cylinder layouts.
s: Uneven running on one cylinder for the first seconds after a cold start
Worse with high ethanol content
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Heater plug at cylinder 4 left loose after intake work
Dead channel 4 in the heater control unit

P23DE.d: P23DE means the cylinder 4 heater control circuit is at a high level where the module expects otherwise. Either the line has contact with a voltage source, or the driving stage no longer switches off, so heater 4 may keep running.
s: Hard restart when the engine is hot
Uneven idle after hot soak
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Channel 4 driver no longer switching off
Cylinder 4 heater line touching a voltage source
Connectors swapped or mismated after repair

P23DF.d: P23DF marks the cylinder 4 heater control circuit as low, which in practice is a short to ground between the control unit and the heater. The channel then stays off until the next start.
s: Rough cold start on one cylinder
Tripped fuel heater fuse
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Chafed insulation on the cylinder 4 heater lead at the rail end
Heating element at cylinder 4 shorted to its housing
Moisture in the cylinder 4 heater plug
Shorted channel 4 output in the heater unit

P23E0.d: P23E0 judges the effect of the cylinder 4 heater rather than its wiring: the circuit is intact, but the heat delivered or the temperature reached falls short of what the conditions call for. One factor specific to resistive heaters is supply voltage.
s: Rough start in cold weather on high-ethanol fuel
Longer cranking
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
c: Aged heater at cylinder 4 with reduced output
Poor contact in the cylinder 4 heater circuit
Weak battery or low system voltage during heating

P23E1.d: P23E1 covers the electrical drive of EGR valve C, a third exhaust gas recirculation actuator next to valves A and B. Which valve carries the letter C is up to the manufacturer; no carmaker documents P23E1 publicly.
s: Warning lamp with otherwise normal driving
Raised NOx at emissions testing
c: Unplugged or corroded connector at EGR valve C
Open motor winding or solenoid coil in valve C
Broken drive wire between engine module and valve C

P23E2.d: P23E2 is raised when the drive circuit of EGR valve C is electrically intact but the valve does not respond to it as expected: commanded and measured position, or drive current and movement, drift apart. In GM's 2018 diesel calibration the A-side check P0404 compares setpoint and measured position of the high-pressure EGR valve and fails above a 10 % tracking error in 152 of 190 samples, with coolant at least 60 °C a
s: Warning lamp after warm-up drives
Occasional hesitation when EGR is cut
c: Soot and lacquer making valve C sluggish
Worn gears or linkage in the valve C actuator
Actuator motor of valve C losing torque

P23E3.d: P23E3 says the control circuit of EGR valve C reads low. On motor or solenoid driven EGR valves this mostly means one of the drive lines has a short to ground, so the output stage would draw excessive current or sees a level it cannot produce by itself.
s: Warning lamp, little change in driving
EGR path C switched off
c: Drive wire of valve C shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve C motor or coil
Faulty output stage in the engine module

P23E4.d: P23E4 is the high counterpart: the control circuit of EGR valve C carries a level that is too high. Typical are a drive line touching a battery feed, a connector pin bent onto a supply terminal, or an output stage that no longer pulls its side low.
s: Warning lamp on
Valve C moves unexpectedly or not at all
c: Drive wire of valve C touching a battery feed
Bent pin in the valve C connector
Engine module output stage not pulling low

P23E5.d: P23E5 means EGR valve C stays open although it is commanded closed. The 2018 GM diesel calibration decides the A-side code P042E like this: once the driver is switched off, the return spring should bring the valve to its closed default within 2 s; if the measured position is still above 5 % after that, the code sets at once as Type A, MIL on the first trip.
s: Rough idle or stalling
Misfire and lack of power
Smoke on diesel engines
Warning lamp on the first trip
c: Carbon deposits holding valve C open
Broken return spring in valve C

P23E6.d: With P23E6 the module concludes that EGR valve C does not open when commanded and stays at or near its closed stop. The consequence is the reverse of P23E5: the engine runs smoothly, but the exhaust share from this path is missing, combustion temperature and NOx go up, and a petrol engine may knock more readily.
s: No change in driving, but higher NOx
Possible knocking on petrol engines
Warning lamp
c: Valve C glued shut by soot
Seized shaft or stripped drive gear
Actuator motor too weak to break the valve free

P23E7.d: P23E7 means the module calculates less recirculated exhaust through path C than it expects for the current operating point. The valve may well move correctly; the gas simply does not get through, for example because the passage, cooler or valve seat is choked with soot.
s: Warning lamp after steady cruising
Raised NOx at emissions testing
c: Soot-choked EGR passage or valve seat on path C
Clogged EGR cooler in path C
Air mass or pressure sensor reading off, skewing the calculation

P23E8.d: P23E8 reports that more exhaust gas passes through the third recirculation path, C, than the module allows for the current operating point – the reverse of P23E7. A valve C that does not seat fully, a leaking bypass or a flow sensor reading too high are the usual explanations.
s: Rough or unstable idle
Engine stalls when coming to a stop
Hesitation or misfire under load
Visible smoke on diesel engines
c: EGR valve C held partly open by carbon deposits
Worn valve seat or leaking bypass in path C
Air-mass or EGR flow sensor reading off, so flow is overestimated

P23E9.d: P23E9 concerns a signal the engine control module sends out rather than one it receives: on some engines the ECM passes a conditioned copy of the bank 2 camshaft A position signal on to another module that needs engine phase information. The code flags a broken or otherwise faulty output line, typically an open circuit found when the driver stage is switched.
s: Stored code with no noticeable change in engine running
Fault entries in the module that receives the camshaft signal
Start-stop or shift functions may be restricted
c: Broken wire in the output line to the receiving module
Terminal pushed back or corroded in a connector
Receiving module unplugged or without its load resistor
Faulty output driver inside the engine control module

P23EA.d: P23EA sets when the ECM's output line that relays the bank 2 camshaft A position signal to another control unit is pulled toward ground. The check is blocked during cranking: the module commands the output high and expects the line to rise; if it stays low, the wire is chafed against ground or the receiver has an internal short.
s: Code stored, engine running normally
Harsher shifts or delayed engagement if the transmission module uses the signal
Start-stop function switched off
c: Output wire chafed through to ground on the engine or body
Receiving module with an input shorted to ground
Moisture or dirt bridging terminals in a connector
Output stage in the engine control module failed

P23EB.d: P23EB is the opposite fault to P23EA: the bank 2 camshaft A output line, which the ECM drives as a switched low-side signal for another module, stays high when it should be pulled low. Typical reasons are a wire touching a supply circuit, moisture in a connector or a defective driver in the ECM.
s: Code present without drivability complaint
Related fault codes in the receiving control module
Comfort functions such as start-stop deactivated
c: Output wire shorted to a battery or 5 V supply wire in the harness
ECM output transistor no longer switching to ground

P23EC.d: P23EC belongs to the camshaft B group – on most layouts the exhaust camshaft – and refers to bank 1, the side with cylinder 1. The ECM rebroadcasts the phase signal of that camshaft on a dedicated output wire, and P23EC reports that this wire, or the driver stage feeding it, shows an open or undefined circuit condition.
s: Stored code, often found during a routine scan
Receiving module runs on substitute values
c: Open circuit in the camshaft B output wire
Connector at the ECM or receiver not fully latched
Input stage of the receiving module defective

P23ED.d: With P23ED the ECM detects that its camshaft B output for bank 1 reads low although it has released the line to go high. Most often a harness section rubbing through to the engine block, a crushed connector pin or a shorted input in the receiving module is to blame.
s: Code stored, engine performance unaffected
Downstream module reports missing camshaft signal
Possible fallback behaviour in transmission or hybrid functions
c: Harness rubbed through against the engine block
Crushed or bent connector pin touching ground
Shorted input in the receiving module

P23EE.d: P23EE flags a camshaft B, bank 1 output line that the ECM cannot pull low: the voltage stays near supply level, pointing to a short to a battery-fed or 5 V wire, a faulty pull-up in the receiving unit or a failed ECM driver transistor. GM documents the test only for the bank 1 camshaft A counterpart P2616 on the 2019 LTG: monitored while the output is commanded low, a short once resistance to power drops to 0.5 ohm o
s: Code logged while the engine runs normally
Faults or reduced functions in the module fed by the signal
c: Output line shorted to a battery or sensor supply wire
Faulty pull-up circuit in the receiving module

P23EF.d: P23EF covers the last combination of this series: camshaft B, usually the exhaust shaft, on bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. On V-engines with four camshafts the ECM can provide a separate phase output per shaft, and P23EF says the bank 2 exhaust output has lost circuit continuity – a broken wire, a terminal backed out of its connector or a missing load at the receiving end.
s: Code stored without warning lamp on many vehicles
Module relying on the signal sets its own fault codes
c: Wire break in the bank 2 camshaft B output line
Terminal backed out of the connector housing
Receiving module disconnected or with failed input

P23F0.d: P23F0 is stored when the bank 2 camshaft B output stays at ground potential while the ECM expects it to float high. A low reading can come from insulation damage near the exhaust side, where heat makes harness sleeves brittle, or from a receiving module whose input has failed shorted.
s: Code stored, engine itself unaffected
Harsher shifts or delayed gear changes
Features such as start-stop disabled
c: Heat-damaged insulation on the exhaust side grounding the wire
Receiving module input failed short to ground
Defective output stage in the ECM

P23F1.d: P23F1 means the camshaft B output for bank 2 sits at a high level that the ECM did not command. Its driver switches the line to ground to form the pulses; if the line stays high while switched, current is coming in from elsewhere – typically a short to a supply wire in a shared harness bundle, sometimes water bridging terminals.
s: Code present, no change in engine behaviour
Communication or plausibility faults in the receiving module
c: Short to a supply wire within a shared harness bundle
Receiving module feeding voltage back into the line

P23F2.d: P23F2 says that the mixture in cylinder 1 has drifted away from the other cylinders and that the control unit holds the second injector of that cylinder, injector B, responsible. Only engines that feed each cylinder through two injectors can produce it.
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable drivability change
Slightly rough idle or a misfire count on cylinder 1
c: Injector B (usually the port injector) of cylinder 1 clogged or dripping
Leaking injector O-ring or intake runner gasket at cylinder 1
Loose connector on injector B of cylinder 1 (often with P21CF)

P23F3.d: P23F3 points to cylinder 2 and to its injector B, the second of two injectors feeding that cylinder. The smallest engines able to raise it have three cylinders, for example Ford's 1.5 EcoBoost, which pairs port and direct injection and can switch one cylinder off at light load.
s: Check engine light on
Shaking at idle, most noticeable on small three- or four-cylinder engines
Slightly higher fuel consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 2 delivering too much or too little fuel
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 2
Work done on the wrong cylinder because of the maker's numbering scheme
Chafed wire to injector B of cylinder 2 (check P21D0)

P23F4.d: P23F4 refers to cylinder 3: the control unit has found that this cylinder burns leaner or richer than the others and traces the deviation to injector B. On a three-cylinder engine with port and direct injection, such as the Ford 1.5 EcoBoost, cylinder 3 is the last one; on four- and six-cylinder engines it lies in the middle of the block or bank.
s: Check engine light on
Possible misfire code P0303 at the same time
Uneven idle when the engine is warm
c: Port injector (injector B) of cylinder 3 dripping or partly blocked
Leaking seal at the intake port of cylinder 3
Low compression or leaking valves on cylinder 3

P23F5.d: P23F5 concerns cylinder 4, the end cylinder of a four-cylinder engine. Many four-cylinder units now carry two injectors per cylinder: Toyota's 8AR-FTS turbo (D-4ST) and its Dynamic Force engines such as the M20A (D-4S), Hyundai's Smartstream G2.5 GDi and T-GDi, and the updated Ford 2.3 EcoBoost of the 2024 Mustang.
s: Check engine light on
Slight vibration at idle
Fuel trim shifted on the single bank
c: Deposits or wear in injector B of cylinder 4
Low-pressure (port) fuel rail problem showing first at cylinder 4 (look for P2BF0/P2BF1)
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 4

P23F6.d: P23F6 flags cylinder 5 and is the first code in this row that a four-cylinder engine can never set. Engines with port plus direct injection and at least five cylinders are mostly V6 and V8 units: Ford's second-generation 3.5 EcoBoost V6, first shown in the 2017 Ford GT, Toyota's 2GR-FKS V6 with D-4S, and the V8s named at P23F8.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in performance
Fuel trim of the affected bank drifts
c: Port injector of cylinder 5 out of tolerance
Intake manifold gasket leaking near cylinder 5
Intermittent contact in the injector B wiring of cylinder 5 (P21D3)

P23F7.d: P23F7 belongs to cylinder 6, the highest-numbered cylinder on a V6 or straight six. Toyota's GR V6 family is a typical carrier: the 2GR-FSE in the Lexus IS and GS and the later 2GR-FKS both use D-4S, in which the port injector supplies part of the fuel next to the direct injector, its share depending on load and engine speed.
s: Check engine light on
Fault comes and goes depending on driving style
Occasional roughness at low or medium load
c: Port injector of cylinder 6 deviating in the ranges where it carries most of the fuel
Air leak at the intake runner or injector seat of cylinder 6
Injection split calibration needing a software update

P23F8.d: P23F8 identifies cylinder 7 and its injector B, so it needs at least seven cylinders, in practice a V8 or V10. Three V8 families using a pair of injectors in every cylinder are on record: Ford's 5.0 Coyote, which gained direct injection on top of port injection for the 2018 Mustang GT and F-150; Toyota's 2UR-GSE with D-4S in Lexus F models and the LC 500; and the supercharged GM LT5 in the 2019 Corvette ZR1, whose po
s: Check engine light on
Fuel trim of one bank off while the other bank is normal
Rarely a perceptible misfire
c: Port injector of cylinder 7 clogged or leaking
Fault in the separate injector B driver module, where fitted (e.g. GM LT5)

P23F9.d: P23F9 points to cylinder 8, the highest number on any V8. GM's 2019 tables for the LT5 Corvette show how far a V8 with port and direct injection resolves imbalance in practice: only bank by bank.
s: Check engine light on
Bank-level imbalance code (P219A/P219B) stored as well
Normal drivability in most cases
c: Injector B of cylinder 8 with wrong flow rate
Leak at the intake runner or PCV connection near cylinder 8
Front oxygen sensor of the bank giving a distorted signal

P23FA.d: P23FA concerns cylinder 9, which among passenger-car engines fitted with dual injection realistically means a V10. The best-known example is the 5.2 litre V10 of the Lamborghini Huracán, described as the first V10 to combine direct and multi-point injection.
s: Check engine light on
Little or no effect on the high-revving engine's behaviour
Bank trim of the second cylinder group shifted
c: Leak in the intake path of cylinder 9
Valve seat or compression problem on cylinder 9

P23FB.d: P23FB marks cylinder 10, the highest cylinder number of a V10. Among dual-injection engines, the Huracán's 5.2 litre unit is the documented case; it adds multi-point injection to direct injection.
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 or misfire code stored alongside
Mostly no noticeable change
c: Port injector of cylinder 10 dirty or worn
Injector seal leaking air at cylinder 10
Heat-damaged wiring to injector B of cylinder 10 (check P21D8)

P23FC.d: P23FC is reserved for cylinder 11, so it can only belong to twelve-cylinder engines that add an extra injector in every cylinder. Such a pairing is hard to find in public engine data.
s: Check engine light on
Hardly any change in smoothness on a twelve-cylinder engine
c: Second injector of cylinder 11 delivering a wrong quantity
Code read from an engine that has no injector B (scan tool or software issue)

P23FD.d: P23FD closes the cylinder series at number 12. It states that the twelfth cylinder runs out of step with the rest and that the cause lies with its injector B.
s: Check engine light on
Bank or misfire code stored at the same time
c: Second injector of cylinder 12 out of tolerance
Intake leak or valve sealing fault at cylinder 12
Code reported by a tool on an engine without a second injector

P23FE.d: P23FE reports a cylinder-to-cylinder imbalance on bank 1 that the control unit attributes to fuel system B, without naming a cylinder. Ford's 2024 OBD summary explains the letter for its dual-injection engines: the port path is Fuel Control System B with its own lean and rich codes (P2BF0/P2BF1 for bank 1), while direct injection forms system A.
s: Check engine light on
Lean or rich fuel trim on bank 1, possibly P2BF0 or P2BF1
Slightly increased fuel consumption
c: Port fuel rail pressure or low-pressure supply wrong on bank 1
Several port injectors on bank 1 fouled by deposits
Intake manifold leak on the bank 1 side
Front oxygen sensor of bank 1 responding poorly

P23FF.d: P23FF mirrors P23FE for bank 2 and can only occur on V, W or boxer engines, because inline engines have no second bank. It means the cylinders on the side without cylinder 1 deviate from each other and the fault is assigned to injection system B, which on Ford's PFDI engines is the port path (lean and rich codes P2BF2/P2BF3).
s: Check engine light on
Fuel trims of the two banks clearly apart
Possibly P2BF2 or P2BF3 as well
c: Several port injectors on bank 2 with deposits or wear
Intake manifold gasket leaking on bank 2
Supply problem in the port fuel rail feeding bank 2
Front oxygen sensor or its wiring on bank 2 distorting the signal
